content: This is a highly detailed and technical document discussing the management of tuberculosis (TB) in children, including drug-resistant TB (DR-TB), and related issues such as maternal and neonatal TB. Adverse effects of anti-TB drugs are less common in children compared to adults. However, when designing a treatment regimen, the risks and benefits of each drug must be carefully evaluated. Caregivers should be informed about potential adverse effects and instructed to report any that occur immediately. No second-line anti-TB drugs are absolutely contraindicated in children, and these drugs should not be withheld unless there is documented hypersensitivity or an intractable adverse reaction. Children treated for drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) generally tolerate second-line drugs well. Regular monitoring of body weight is essential, as drug dosages need to be adjusted as the child gains weight. Baseline audiometry and monthly hearing tests are mandatory for children receiving Group 2 injectable agents, particularly aminoglycosides, due to the risk of ototoxicity. This is especially important for high-risk patients, such as those with diabetes, HIV, or renal insufficiency. For children with DR-TB who are also HIV-positive, additional management includes the administration of pyridoxine (5–10 mg/kg per day), cotrimoxazole preventive therapy (CPT), and antiretroviral therapy (ART), which significantly improves treatment outcomes and should be initiated as early as possible. Corticosteroids may be used as indicated for drug-susceptible TB and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Adherence to treatment is crucial to prevent further development of drug resistance. Adverse effects associated with firstand second-line anti-TB drugs in children include hepatotoxicity, jaundice, rash, and peripheral neuropathy (rare) for isoniazid; hepatotoxicity, jaundice, arthralgia, and rash for pyrazinamide; and optic neuritis (rare) for ethambutol, which requires vision screening if possible. Injectable agents (Group 2) such as amikacin, kanamycin, and capreomycin carry risks of ototoxicity (starting with high-frequency hearing loss), nephrotoxicity, and severe hypokalemia, necessitating regular hearing tests and monitoring of serum creatinine and potassium levels. Fluoroquinolones (Group 3) may cause gastrointestinal disturbances, insomnia, and arthralgia, with serum uric acid monitoring recommended when used with pyrazinamide. Second-line oral drugs (Group 4) like ethionamide and prothionamide can cause gastrointestinal disturbances, hepatotoxicity, and hypothyroidism, requiring clinical observation and monitoring of thyroid function tests. Cycloserine and terizidone may lead to psychosis, convulsions, and depression, while para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) can cause gastrointestinal disturbances and hypothyroidism. Third-line drugs (Group 5), such as linezolid, may result in myelosuppression, lactic acidosis, peripheral neuropathy, and pancreatitis, requiring close clinical and laboratory monitoring. Adherence to both anti-TB treatment and ART is critical, despite challenges such as the unpleasant taste of some drugs, nausea, vomiting, and the large number of oral medications required. Injectable drugs, if necessary, should be administered daily at a local health clinic. Directly observed therapy (DOT) is essential for DR-TB treatment, and in some cases, hospitalization may be required until the completion of injectable therapy. Vomiting caused by thioamides and PAS can often be managed by splitting the daily dose initially or starting with a lower dose and gradually increasing to the full dose over 1–2 weeks. Single daily doses should be reinstated once vomiting resolves. Children undergoing treatment for TB should be monitored for three key reasons: to assess their response to therapy, to identify adverse events early, and to promote adherence. A monitoring schedule, as suggested by Seddon et al., can be adapted to local conditions and resources. National tuberculosis programs (NTPs) are responsible for implementing childhood TB activities in line with national guidelines. This includes integrating TB care into maternal and child health services and ensuring accurate recording and reporting of TB cases in children. All children treated for TB should be registered in the NTP system, with data recorded on age, type of TB, HIV status, and use of CPT and ART if HIV-positive. Cohort analysis of treatment outcomes in children is a valuable indicator of program quality. Pregnancy increases the risk of TB disease in previously infected women, particularly in the third trimester or early postpartum period. Maternal TB is a significant cause of maternal mortality in TB/HIV-endemic settings. Pregnant women in TB-endemic regions should be screened for TB symptoms, and those with suspected TB should also be tested for HIV. Prompt treatment of TB in pregnancy is essential to prevent transmission and improve outcomes. The treatment regimen for TB in pregnant women is similar to that for non-pregnant women, except for streptomycin, which is contraindicated in pregnancy. HIV-positive pregnant women with TB should receive ART according to WHO guidelines. Congenital TB, acquired in utero or during delivery, typically presents within the first three weeks of life and has a high mortality rate. Diagnosis should include a thorough maternal history of TB or HIV infection. Management of neonatal TB should be conducted by an experienced clinician, with prompt initiation of treatment based on suspicion while awaiting bacteriological confirmation. Standard WHO-recommended drug regimens for drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB should be used, with dosages adjusted for body weight and weight gain. Breastfeeding is recommended regardless of the mother’s TB status, as the risk of TB transmission through breast milk is negligible. Separation of the mother and infant is not advised unless the mother has multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) or the infant is acutely ill. Neonates exposed to maternal TB should be screened for TB disease, and if asymptomatic, they should receive isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) for six months, followed by a tuberculin skin test (TST). BCG vaccination should be delayed until TB disease is excluded and the TST is negative. National TB programs should integrate TB prevention, diagnosis, and treatment into maternal, neonatal, and child health services, particularly in high TB/HIV prevalence settings. This includes regular TB screening for pregnant women living with HIV and the implementation of integrated patient monitoring systems for TB, HIV, and prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) services. Training and supervision of health workers are essential to improve case finding, management, and preventive therapy for childhood TB, as well as to enhance recording and reporting practices. Training should focus on identifying children with suspected TB, managing TB in the community, and screening close contacts of TB cases.
